records.title: Cultural Adaptation of an Intervention Guide for a Non-pharmacological Palliative Care Intervention for People With Advanced Dementia: A Multi-Stakeholder Process Preparatory to the International In-Touch Trial
records.abstract: Effective, internationally transferable interventions for people with advanced dementia are needed to enhance consistent, high-quality care and quality of life. The international In-Touch project includes a cluster randomised controlled trial of an intervention to improve the quality of life for people with advanced dementia within nursing homes. A structured cultural adaptation process is crucial to ensure the In-Touch intervention retains core principles while improving local feasibility and acceptability, thereby enabling a clear assessment of fidelity. Here, we detail the cultural adaptation of the ‘In-Touch Practical Guide for Nursing Home Staff’ to enhance its feasibility, usability, and relevance across nursing homes in seven European countries. A structured cultural adaptation process, inspired by the ADAPT framework, was guided by an international team of experts, including individuals with lived experience, and dementia and palliative care researchers. Within-country group interviews were conducted in the Czech Republic, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Portugal, the Netherlands and the UK with three key participant groups: (1) nursing home staff familiar with intervention components, (2) nursing home staff unfamiliar with the intervention, and (3) family carers of people with advanced dementia. Participants ( n = 97) evaluated the guide’s clarity, cultural appropriateness, and feasibility. Cross-country consensus is presented here, with key themes including the need to simplify the guide to improve usability, ensure accessible language for all staff levels, and introduce discussion of flexibility in session length, structure, and available spaces to align with nursing home routines. Clearer guidance was needed on the roles of volunteers and family members. The guide was refined into a single, adaptable version, optimising its cultural relevance, usability, and practicality across diverse European settings. This collaborative adaptation process led to a culturally sensitive guide optimised for use in the In-Touch trial across Europe. The outlined  can help adapt other interventions for future international palliative care research.

records.title: Physical Functioning, Crime, and Cognitive Decline in Mexican Americans: A Multi-Level Analysis of Protective Interactions
records.abstract: Hispanic individuals are understudied in cognitive aging research and are disproportionately exposed to crime, yet the cognitive consequences of this exposure remain unclear. We examined whether county-level crime moderates the association between physical functioning (PF) and cognitive change among Mexican Americans aged 75 years and older without cognitive impairment at baseline.  Participants included 1,189 older adults from the Hispanic Established Populations for the Epidemiologic Study of the Elderly (HEPESE). Cognitive functioning was measured using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), PF was assessed using performance-based measures, and total crime was measured at the county level. Multilevel models adjusted for demographic, socioeconomic, and cardiovascular factors.  Better PF was associated with higher MMSE scores. A significant interaction among PF, crime, and time indicated that the protective association between PF and cognitive functioning weakened as county-level crime increased. Higher PF predicted less cognitive decline in low- and moderate-crime areas, although this association was attenuated in moderate-crime contexts and largely absent in high-crime areas. Discussion County-level crime may undermine the cognitive benefits of better PF in late life. These findings underscore the role of contextual factors in cognitive aging among older Mexican Americans and highlight potential targets for community-level prevention efforts.

records.title: Cognitive trajectories before and after the Global Financial Crisis: a 20-year cohort study of older adults in Australia
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Macroeconomic shocks may influence cognitive function in later life. We examined cognitive trajectories around the 2007-2009 Global Financial Crisis (GFC) among older Australians and whether resilience factors modified these trajectories.  We used longitudinal data from 1,872 community-dwelling adults in the 60-66-year cohort of the PATH Through Life Study. Participants were followed from 2001-2002 to 2020-2021 across six waves (∼4-year intervals). Perceived financial impact of the GFC and co-occurring distress/anxiety were assessed at wave 3 (2009-2010) and categorised as no impact, impact without distress/anxiety, and impact with distress/anxiety. A global cognitive composite was calculated and standardised as z-scores. Linear mixed-effects models estimated pre-GFC change, change during the GFC, and post-GFC change. Effect modification by 13 resilience factors was examined.  Most reported no financial impact (66.2%); 23.8% reported impact without distress/anxiety, and 10.0% with distress/anxiety. Pre-GFC cognitive decline was similar across groups. During the GFC, all groups experienced a decline (-0.057 to -0.091 SD). During the post-GFC period, cognition declined further at similar rates in the no impact, impact without distress/anxiety, and impact with distress/anxiety groups: -0.073 SD/year (95% CI: -0.080, -0.066), -0.070 (-0.079, -0.060), and -0.069 (-0.083, -0.056), respectively. Higher physical health-related quality of life attenuated the decline during the GFC, while greater life satisfaction and positive social support were associated with slower post-GFC decline. Discussion Cognitive decline increased around the GFC period and continued thereafter, with no evidence that these changes differed by perceived financial impact or distress/anxiety. Causal attribution to the GFC is limited by the absence of an unexposed comparison group.

records.title: Preparing for the future, feeling better now: Old-age financial preparation and psychological well-being in pre-old-age Korean adults
records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Population aging has made old-age financial preparation increasingly consequential, yet it is typically indexed by a single measure that does not distinguish among the forms it takes. Drawing on Conservation of Resources theory and the institutional and normative structure of retirement in Korea, we examined associations between within-person changes in financial preparation and two distinct dimensions of subjective well-being among pre-old-age Korean adults.  Using seven biennial waves (2011–2023) of the Korean Retirement and Income Study (9,887 person-waves; 2,389 individuals), we estimated individual fixed-effects regressions examining associations between old-age financial preparation and depressive symptoms, measured using the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), and life satisfaction, adjusting for key time-varying covariates.  Within-person transitions into preparation were associated with a 1.02-point lower CES-D score and a 0.11-point higher life-satisfaction score on a 5-point scale (both p Discussion Old-age financial preparation appears to function as a within-person psychosocial resource related to both evaluative and affective dimensions of well-being. These divergent patterns suggest that the scope and adequacy of preparation matter differently for depressive symptoms and global life evaluations, potentially informing pension policy and financial-planning interventions in aging societies.

records.title: Co-Creating Dementia Education: What People Living With Dementia Want Health and Social Care Professionals to Know
records.abstract: There is growing recognition that high-quality dementia education must be shaped by the expertise of those with lived experience. While people with dementia are increasingly involved in the development and delivery of dementia education, decisions about curriculum structure and priorities often remain led by academics with learned rather than lived experience. This paper addresses that gap by placing people with dementia at the centre of curriculum creation. In partnership with educators, people with dementia shared their insights into what health and social care professionals need to know, understand, and enact in practice to provide effective care. Nineteen online workshops were conducted with 22 people living with dementia in the United Kingdom, and two academics over an 18-month period (between January 2022 and September 2023). Three priority areas were identified, refined and validated through an iterative consensus process and thematic analysis: (1) Challenging stigma, stereotypes, and discrimination; (2) Seeing the individual and providing person-centred care; and (3) Enhancing language and communication. These priorities became the foundation of a new postgraduate module co-created through lived and learned experience. To examine how the priorities identified by people with dementia align with existing national expectations for dementia education, the themes were mapped against the Dementia Training Standards Framework (DTSF). There was strong alignment with key framework domains, particularly equality and inclusion, person-centred care, and communication, while also highlighting meaningful gaps. The co-created priorities emphasised critical reflection on professional assumptions, intersectional stigma and rights-based practice across all levels of training. The findings demonstrate how people living with dementia can play a central role in shaping dementia education, identifying priorities that both align with and extend existing curriculum standards. They highlight the value of merging lived and learned experience to ensure dementia education reflects what matters most to those living with the condition.

records.title: Use of Digital Tools and Environmental Practices Among Informal Caregivers of Older Adults in the European Union Embracing the Triple Transition: Cross-Sectional Study
records.abstract: The European Union is currently facing a demographic, digital, and environmental transition collectively known as the triple transition. Although these trends significantly impact long-term care services, they have typically been studied in isolation, overlooking potential synergies between the adoption of digital tools and environmental practices among informal caregivers of older adults. This study uniquely bridges this gap by applying an integrative social-ecological-infrastructural systems framework to examine how these transitions interact in everyday caregiving contexts.  This study examined the relationship between the use of digital tools and eco-friendly practices among informal caregivers of older adults across the European Union and whether the adoption of digital solutions related differently to specific types of eco-friendly behaviors. Unlike previous research focusing on isolated aspects of each transition, we examined their interconnections, providing empirical evidence for developing integrated policy approaches.  Using data from the Survey of Gender Gaps in Unpaid Care, Individual and Social Activities project (n=5761 informal caregivers of adults aged ≥65 years), we analyzed the association between frequency of use of digital tools for caregiving and environmental practices. We used the social-ecological-infrastructural systems conceptual framework and the theory of planned behavior (TPB) to interpret findings. Analyses included descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, and multilevel mixed-effects regression models.  A weak positive association was observed between the frequency of use of digital tools and environmentally sustainable behaviors (ρ=0.28; P P =.23) and mindful consumption of natural resources (ρ=−0.02; P >.99). Respondents using digital tools daily had scores of environmentally sustainable behavior (SESBs) 22% higher than nonusers. Demographic patterns revealed higher use of digital tools among younger, more educated, and employed caregivers, indicating that any potential digital-environmental co-occurrence may be unevenly distributed across the caregiver population.  The use of digital tools may be related to environmental behavior through improved access to information, peer norms, and a greater perceived ability to act, though these mechanisms were not directly tested. The stronger associations with consumption-related behaviors indicate that digital platforms may be particularly relevant to caregivers’ access to eco-friendly products, second-hand goods, fair-trade options, and sustainable local services. By contrast, the lack of statistically significant correlations with recycling and resource conservation suggests that digital solutions alone may be insufficient to address behaviors that depend on structural conditions, physical infrastructure, local service availability, or established household routines. Policies should consider digital inclusion, caregiver support, and green infrastructure as interconnected areas while ensuring that older, less educated, and more burdened caregivers are not excluded from these potential co-benefits.

records.title: Invisible labor, relational lives: Poetic inquiry into women of color navigating dual-role caregiving
records.abstract: AbstractR  and  Qualitative  are foundational to gerontological research, yet conventional analytic approaches may obscure the relational, moral, and embodied dimensions of caregiving that unfold across aging care systems. Women of color employed in long-term care who also provide unpaid caregiving inhabit intersecting landscapes of care that remain under-described. This study responds to calls for methodological innovation in gerontology by advancing poetic inquiry as a rigorous qualitative approach for illuminating caregiving across institutional and domestic contexts. Research Design and  Guided by feminist ethics and intersectionality, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight women of color working in long-term care who also identified as family caregivers. Using a voice-centered relational approach, I-Poems were constructed from transcripts to preserve first-person language, temporal flow, and meaning. Grounded in the Listening Guide, analysis emphasized relational listening, reflexivity, and attentiveness to marginalized voices, positioning poems as both analytic products and ethical encounters.  The I-Poems illuminate caregiving as intersubjective, continuous, and morally grounded, characterized by blurred boundaries between paid and unpaid care, work and home, self and other, and obligation and choice. Care emerged not as discrete roles but as a way of being-with others across aging contexts.  The findings challenge work–life balance discourses and call for relationally attuned workplace policies that recognize caregiving as socially embedded and valued labor. By demonstrating poetic inquiry as a methodological and ethical innovation, this study expands analytic possibilities for research on caregiving and aging and is generative for future studies with underrepresented populations.

records.title: Digital Inclusion as a Context-Dependent Mediating Pathway Between Social Isolation and Cognitive Functioning in Chinese and European Older Adults
records.abstract: Social isolation is a modifiable risk factor for cognitive decline in older adults, but the mediating role of digital inclusion across settings remains unclear. We integrated a Chinese cross-sectional study (DIHA, 2024), two longitudinal cohorts (CHARLS and SHARE), and two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) using European-ancestry genome-wide data. Four-way decomposition assessed mediation through internet access or use and exposure-mediator interaction. Among 18,071 adults aged ≥55 years, social isolation was associated with poorer cognition across cohorts. Longitudinal mediation was clearest in SHARE, particularly for lack of group participation, but was not significant in CHARLS; DIHA mediation findings were cross-sectional and exploratory. MR linked genetically predicted loneliness and fewer leisure social activities to poorer cognition, providing complementary evidence. Digital inclusion may contribute to the relationship between social isolation and cognitive ageing, with its role warranting further investigation across settings.

records.title: Behind Closed Doors: Caregiving Burden in Exclusive Two-Person Living Arrangements
records.abstract: This study examined caregiving burden among primary family caregivers in two-person households, consisting solely of home-based Long-Term Care Insurance recipients and their caregivers in South Korea. By analyzing 1,068 caregivers from the 2019 and 2022 Korean Long-Term Care Surveys (717 spouses; 351 adult children), we assessed burden across emotional support, IADL, housekeeping, and physical ADL domains. Spousal caregivers showed higher odds of IADL and physical ADL burden, and caregiving frequency was positively associated with their emotional support and housekeeping burden. Adult child caregivers were more likely to experience burden when caring for male or dementia-affected recipients. These findings suggest that burden was linked to caregiving frequency among spouses and to recipient characteristics among adult children. Spousal caregivers may face greater strain from age-related limitations and continuous care demands. Recipient-centered policies may not adequately address their needs; caregiver-inclusive assessments and targeted support merit consideration.

records.title: Depression Management: Daily Practice in Dutch and Flemish Nursing Homes
records.abstract: Despite the numerous guidelines and training programs, depression remains highly prevalent among nursing home residents.  Exploring depression care strategies currently applied in nursing homes.  A cross-sectional observational study.  204 residents from 46 care units (21 Dutch and 25 Flemish) participated. Approximately one in five participating residents had an official depression diagnosis. Regular screening and monitoring procedures were reported in 17 (37%) care units and established in one in five participants. Depression management was organized in multidisciplinary teams. Non-pharmacological interventions, such as restructuring daily schedules and offering pleasant/meaningful activities, were frequently employed. Evaluation procedures were conducted in 26 (56%) of the care units and established in one in five participants. Clinical and statistical relevant regional differences in depression care strategies were found at the nursing homes’ unit level.  Depression remains prevalent among nursing home residents. Areas for improving depression care included monitoring, screening, and evaluating procedures.

records.title: Hearing assistance technologies and social health among individuals with care and support needs: a scoping review
records.abstract: Hearing loss can affect communication, social interaction, participation, and the maintenance of social relationships, particularly among individuals who require care or support in everyday life. Hearing assistance technologies (HATs) may facilitate communication, but their relationship with the multiple dimensions of social health remains insufficiently understood. A multidimensional social-health framework encompassing Capacity, Independence, Social Participation, Structure, Function, and Appraisal provides a basis for examining these relationships beyond individual hearing outcomes. This scoping review aimed to map the existing evidence on HATs in relation to social health among individuals with care and support needs.  This scoping review followed the PRISMA-ScR guidelines and the methodological framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley and further refined by Levac. PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, the Cochrane Library, Ovid MEDLINE, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore were searched. Studies were eligible if they included individuals aged ≥ 18 years with care and support needs and examined HATs in relation to findings relevant to social health. Data were charted and synthesised descriptively, and findings were organised according to the six domains of the multidimensional social-health framework, comprising Capacity, Independence, Social Participation, Structure, Function, and Appraisal.  The searches identified 1,145 records, of which 21 studies met the inclusion criteria. The included samples were predominantly older. Findings were most frequently mapped to the Appraisal and Social Participation domains, whereas Structure and Function were comparatively underrepresented. Intervention findings included improvements in communication-related outcomes and reductions in hearing-related participation restrictions, whereas findings for loneliness, relationship satisfaction, social-network characteristics, and broader social engagement were less consistent. Qualitative findings highlighted stigma and perceived social judgement, with the social acceptability of hearing technologies also described in relation to everyday interaction and technology use.  Evidence on HATs in relation to social health among individuals with care and support needs remains heterogeneous and uneven across social-health domains. Limited attention to the structural and functional dimensions of social relationships highlights the need for more comprehensive assessment of social health in hearing-care research. Future studies should adopt longitudinal, network-sensitive, and culturally responsive approaches and consider the interpersonal, environmental, and care contexts in which HATs are used.

records.title: Insomnia symptoms, daytime sleepiness, and quality of life in people with Alzheimer’s disease: a secondary cross-sectional analysis
records.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but the relation of insomnia symptoms and daytime sleepiness to patient-reported quality of life (QoL) remains uncertain, particularly in people with substantial cognitive impairment. We examined exploratory associations with four QoL domains.  This secondary cross-sectional analysis included 70 participants aged 60–94 years with clinically diagnosed AD recruited from nursing homes and community-based support services in Kraków, Poland. Insomnia symptoms were assessed using the Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS), daytime sleepiness using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), and QoL using the World Health Organization Quality of Life–Brief Version (WHOQOL-BREF). Cognitive impairment was assessed using an abbreviated version of the Blessed Dementia Scale (BDS). Associations between sleep measures and the Physical Health, Psychological, Social Relationships, and Environment domains of the WHOQOL-BREF were examined using Spearman correlations and multivariable linear regression. AIS and ESS were entered simultaneously into the regression models, which were adjusted for age, sex, continuous abbreviated BDS score, depressive symptoms, functional status, and care setting. HC3 robust standard errors were used, and the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure was applied across eight prespecified sleep–QoL associations.  Participants were aged 60–94 years, with a mean age of 78.5 ± 7.9 years, and 45.7% were women. The mean AIS score was 9.31 ± 4.01, with 80.0% of participants meeting the AIS threshold for clinically relevant insomnia symptoms. The mean ESS score was 8.91 ± 2.83, and 30.0% had excessive daytime sleepiness. AIS and ESS scores were positively correlated (Spearman’s ρ = 0.622, p p = 0.027; FDR q = 0.128), whereas greater insomnia symptom severity was nominally associated with poorer Psychological QoL (B = − 0.512, 95% CI − 0.980 to − 0.044; p = 0.032; FDR q = 0.128). Neither association remained statistically significant after FDR correction. No adjusted associations of AIS or ESS with the Social Relationships or Environment domains were observed. The direction of the two principal associations was maintained in expanded and influence sensitivity analyses.  In this exploratory sample, two adjusted associations were nominally significant, but neither survived correction for eight comparisons. Overlap among questionnaire constructs, uncertainty in self-report with cognitive impairment, and the modest sample size limit interpretation. Larger studies with documented response assistance and complementary sleep assessments are needed. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

records.title: Building diverse participatory research teams in falls prevention: a qualitative interview study
records.abstract: An important area of participatory research and the establishment of participatory research teams (PRT) is falls prevention, as falls pose significant risks not only to individuals but also to healthcare systems worldwide. However, little is known about how PRTs are conducted within falls prevention research. Therefore, this study aimed to identify key factors that facilitate participatory research in this context.  The PRT was involved in two projects, focusing on falls prevention: iSeFallED and TRAIL. We conducted eleven semi-structured interviews with each member of the PRT (six patient representatives, five health service representatives). The interviews were transcribed and then analyzed using qualitative content analysis.  Heterogeneous , communication grounded in values such as mutual respect, opportunities for networking, knowledge exchange, and intrinsic motivation were identified as important facilitators.  This study provides insights into key factors for implementing participatory research in falls prevention. Trial registration TRAIL NCT06652828, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06652828#more-information , registered on 21stOctober 2024, and iSeFallED DRKS00035322, https://drks.de/search/de/trial/DRKS00035322 , Registered on 5th March 2025.

records.title: The Influencing Factors and Their Mechanisms of Retirement Planning for Middle-Aged and Older Adults: Explanation of the Mediating Effect of Subjective Life Expectancy
records.abstract: Global population aging and delayed retirement policies make understanding retirement planning essential. Using 2020 CHARLS data ( n = 7,163; aged 45–64), this study found that only 35.3% of participants had a retirement plan (mean horizon: 8.5 years). Chronic diseases such as diabetes and memory disorders reduced retirement planning intentions by lowering subjective life expectancy (SLE). Notably, non-agricultural employment was associated with a higher likelihood of retirement planning partly through higher SLE. Although non-agricultural workers tended to anticipate earlier retirement, their higher SLE was indirectly associated with later planned retirement. SLE may also be a relevant psychological indicator of retirement planning in other aging societies, although cross-national validation is needed.

records.title: “ I have Alzheimer’s disease, it doesn’t have me ”. Words of Wisdom From People Living With Dementia: A Secondary Qualitative Analysis
records.abstract: Receiving a diagnosis of dementia can be an unsettling experience, often complicated by a lack of hope when seeking resources and support. While clinical guidance is important, peer-to-peer knowledge shared among people living with dementia can provide meaningful insight into ways to support one’s well-being. The Wisdom Series was a three-part webinar series designed and offered by people living with dementia for people living with dementia. Led by a dementia advocate who lives with dementia, the series provided a platform for 17 individuals living with dementia across Canada to share their experiences and strategies for living well with dementia with others. A secondary qualitative data analysis was conducted with transcripts of the Wisdom Series webinars to understand participants’ perspectives on well-being. Using thematic analysis, six themes were identified: (1) Knowing Yourself: Recognizing Abilities and Limits, highlighting the importance of adaptation and self-awareness; (2) Connecting with Meaningful Supports, focusing on relationships with peers, family, and animals; (3) Keeping your Mind and Body Nourished and Active, emphasizing cognitive, physical, and holistic approaches to health; (4) Finding Joy in Nature, illustrating emotional benefits of engaging with the natural environment; (5) Supporting Self and Others through Advocacy, describing participants’ efforts to improve accessibility and awareness in their communities; and (6) Planning for the Future, encompassing advance care planning, medical assistance in dying, autonomy, and burden. In sharing their experiences and perspectives, the webinar panellists not only shared their wisdom but challenged deficit-based assumptions about dementia by demonstrating the agency, citizenship, and personhood of people living with dementia.

records.title: Machine Learning–Based Biomechanical and Clinical Assessment of the Five Times Chair Rise Test in Older Adults: Sensor-Based Functional Aging Study
records.abstract: Maintaining functional ability is essential for healthy aging. The Five Times Chair Rise Test (5CRT) is widely used to assess lower-extremity function, yet conventional stopwatch timing provides limited insight into movement quality and compensatory strategies. Sensor-based biomechanics combined with machine learning (ML) enables detailed analysis of movement dynamics and supports digital health approaches for early detection and monitoring of functional decline. However, the clinical relevance of ML-based 5CRT movement patterns and their relationship to established functional outcomes and aging trajectories remains insufficiently understood.  This study aimed (1) to classify 5CRT movement patterns using an established dynamic time warping (DTW)-based clustering workflow; (2) to examine associations between ML-based movement clusters and multidimensional indicators of strength, mobility, and functional performance across 24 months; and (3) to evaluate whether ML-based movement classification provides clinically meaningful differentiation beyond conventional stopwatch-based 5CRT timing within a digital health assessment context.  In this longitudinal observational study, community-dwelling adults aged ≥70 years completed standardized functional assessments at baseline, 6 months, and 24 months, including Handgrip Strength, Stair Climb Power Test, Timed “Up & Go” Test, Short Physical Performance Battery (including 5CRT), 4-meter Gait Speed, Balance Testing, 6-minute Walking Test, and Countermovement Jump. The assessments were recorded using a force plate and depth camera to capture biomechanical time-series data. DTW and k-means clustering were applied to ground reaction force signals to identify movement patterns.  Among 172 participants included in the final analysis (mean age 76.9, SD 3.40 years; 96/172, 56% female), 2 distinct movement clusters were identified. Cluster 1 demonstrated faster chair rise performance and lower stabilization forces, whereas cluster 2 exhibited slower execution and increased stabilization demands. Across baseline, 6-month, and 24-month follow-up assessments, cluster 1 consistently showed higher muscle strength, greater leg power, faster mobility, higher gait speed, and longer walking distance than cluster 2 (all P  ML-based analysis of sensor-based chair rise performance identifies functional performance profiles beyond conventional timing metrics. Integrating biomechanical movement analytics into digital health assessment frameworks may improve early detection of mobility decline and support longitudinal monitoring and personalized intervention planning in older adults.

records.title: From Digital Engagement to in-Person Social Participation: Examining Associations Between Online Activities and Multiple Indicators of Social Participation Among Older Adults in Germany
records.abstract: Digital involvement shapes aging, with both positive and negative effects. This study examines how different Internet use types (social, information-seeking, entertainment) relate to older adults’ social participation, considering both  (social activity level) and perceived social participation (loneliness and sense of mattering i.e., feeling important to others). Furthermore, this study examined whether digital skills moderate the associations between Internet use and social participation outcomes. Cross-sectional data from 426 community-dwelling adults aged 50-95 (M = 69.1) in Germany were analyzed using hierarchical linear regressions and moderation analyses. Social use and information-seeking were positively associated with  social participation, while media streaming showed a negative association. More frequent social Internet use was associated with lower loneliness. Higher digital skill levels strengthened the negative association between social Internet use and loneliness. The findings suggest distinct associations between different types of Internet use and social participation, with digital skills potentially moderating these associations in later life.

records.title: Multidimensional frailty trajectories and associated factors in older adults with pulmonary tuberculosis: a prospective longitudinal study
records.abstract: Older adults with pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) are particularly vulnerable to multidimensional frailty. However, longitudinal evidence regarding patterns of frailty changes after antituberculosis treatment initiation and their associated factors remains limited. This study aimed to identify distinct trajectories of multidimensional frailty among older adults with pulmonary TB and to examine the associations of anxiety, depression, insomnia, and clinical characteristics with different frailty trajectories.  A prospective longitudinal study was conducted among 251 older adults with pulmonary TB. Multidimensional frailty was assessed using the Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI) at 1, 3, 9, and 12 months after initiation of antituberculosis treatment. At baseline, anxiety and depression were assessed using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), and insomnia was assessed using the Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS). Latent class growth analysis was used to identify distinct trajectories of multidimensional frailty. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was subsequently applied to select candidate variables, followed by multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with trajectory membership.  Three distinct trajectories of multidimensional frailty were identified: high-frailty decreasing (13.1%), moderate-frailty improving (17.9%), and low-frailty persistent (68.9%) trajectory. Multinomial LASSO regression selected 14 candidate variables potentially associated with frailty trajectory membership. Compared with the low-frailty persistence trajectory, a history of smoking (OR = 4.668, 95% CI 1.217–7.904, P = 0.025) was associated with greater odds of membership in the high-frailty decreasing trajectory. records.title: Timed Up and Go, gait speed, and grip strength: associations and discriminative performance for falls in community-dwelling older adults - results from the KORA-age study
records.abstract: Physical performance measures are commonly used in geriatric assessment and have been associated with falls, but their ability to discriminate between older adults with and without falls may be limited. We compared the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test, gait speed, and grip strength within a population-based cohort, considering associations, discriminatory performance, incremental discrimination, and established clinical TUG thresholds.  We analyzed data from 1,079 community-dwelling adults aged ≥ 65 years participating in KORA-Age. Fall status was classified for 819 participants based on self-reported falls in the 12 months preceding the 3-year follow-up interview. Associations of baseline TUG, gait speed, and grip strength with reported falls were examined using sequential logistic regression models adjusted for age and sex, additional clinical covariates, and frailty. Discriminatory performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with DeLong tests used to evaluate incremental discrimination beyond age and sex. We additionally examined combinations of the three performance measures and predefined TUG thresholds. Inverse-probability weighting was used in sensitivity analyses to address selective follow-up.  Poorer TUG performance remained associated with reported falls after additional adjustment for frailty (OR per 1-s increase 1.095, 95% CI 1.018–1.176), whereas the association with slower gait speed was attenuated after frailty adjustment and grip strength was not associated with falls. The age- and sex-adjusted reference model had an AUC of 0.680; corresponding AUCs after adding TUG, gait speed, or grip strength were 0.700, 0.692, and 0.675, respectively, with no clear evidence of incremental discrimination. Combining all three performance measures did not improve discrimination beyond TUG alone. Higher TUG thresholds identified smaller groups with a higher prevalence of falls and greater specificity but progressively lower sensitivity. Inverse-probability-weighted analyses yielded similar associations.  TUG remained associated with reported falls after multivariable and additional frailty adjustment, but none of the three physical performance measures showed clear incremental discrimination beyond age and sex. Combining the measures did not improve discrimination, and established TUG thresholds showed limited sensitivity. These findings support distinguishing statistical associations with falls from the ability of physical performance measures to discriminate between older adults with and without falls. records.journal: The Journals of Gerontology, Series B: Psychological Sciences and Social Sciences
records.abstract: Socioeconomic inequalities in depressive symptoms are well documented, yet little is known about how these inequalities unfold during midlife and whether they vary across national and historical contexts.  Using harmonized longitudinal data spanning 1992 to 2022 from 16 countries (United States, England, France, Austria, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland, Israel, Italy, Spain, Greece, Denmark, Netherlands, Sweden, South Korea, and China), this study modeled trajectories of depressive symptoms among adults aged 45 to 65 across four wealth-based socioeconomic strata: Low (1st to 15th percentile), Lower-middle (16th to 45th), Upper-middle (46th to 75th), and High (76th to 100th).   revealed cross-national disparities: midlife adults in the United States reported higher depressive symptoms than their peers in most other nations, and this difference was most pronounced among lower SES groups. In most nations, later-born cohorts reported more depressive symptoms, with Upper-middle SES individuals exhibiting the largest historical increases. Beyond these mean-level patterns, lower SES groups were found to exhibit greater heterogeneity across three trajectory features of depressive symptoms (i.e., mean-levels at age 50 as well as linear and quadratic changes in depressive symptoms). This may suggest that under socioeconomic disadvantage, depressive symptoms are less tightly structured by SES alone and more strongly shaped by other contextual and individual factors. Discussion Collectively, findings highlight that mental health inequalities in midlife are deeply embedded in societal and historically changing structures. Policies that strengthen social protections and promote economic security may reduce these disparities and enhance well-being across the life course.

records.title: Temporal Trends in the Prevalence of Frailty in England From 2002 to 2022, With Forecasts to 2040: Longitudinal Secondary Analysis of a National Cohort Study
records.abstract: The increasing life expectancy provides an opportunity for healthy longevity, but frailty is a potential challenge. Existing studies of frailty prevalence in England are largely cross-sectional, use heterogeneous frailty definitions, and rarely break down population-level drivers or project future burden, limiting their use for health and social care planning.  This study aimed to explore temporal trends of frailty prevalence and project scenario-based future prevalence up to 2040 for the community-dwelling population aged 50 years and older in England.  Prevalence of frailty (measured using a frailty index) in the overall sample and subgroups of age, sex, educational level, and marital status from 2002 to 2022 was estimated among the community-dwelling population aged 50 years and older using 10 waves of nationally representative data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA; n=6226 to 11,218 across waves). The number of individuals with frailty was also derived in each year. Joinpoint regression models were used to explore temporal trends of frailty prevalence. A linear probability regression model was performed using pooled data from 10 waves of the ELSA to explore driving factors and project future prevalence. Decomposition analysis was used to estimate the contribution of individual factors to the change in prevalence.  A statistically nonsignificant ( P =.61) increase of 2.3 percentage points from 15.5% (1738/11,218) in 2002 to 17.8% (1108/6226) in 2022 was observed, with the number of individuals with frailty growing from 2,560,122 to 3,791,038 among community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older in England. Those with advanced age, who were female, had a lower educational level, and/or were single had a consistently higher prevalence of frailty. Opposing contributions netted to this overall change: improvements in sociodemographic conditions and educational attainment and healthier lifestyle behaviors offset 222.5%, 94.9%, and 51.6% of the observed increase, respectively. Under scenario-based projections, prevalence was estimated at 20.5% (95% CI 19.2%-21.9%) in 2040, corresponding to 5,213,689 people with frailty.  Despite a modest increase in prevalence among the community-dwelling population aged 50 years and older, the substantial growth in the absolute number of individuals with frailty indicates a likely rise in future care demands. The study contributes a 20-year trend, decomposition, and forecast framework for community-dwelling older adults. Findings support prioritizing broader sociodemographic development alongside educational attainment and healthy lifestyles, with potential policy approaches including income and social protection, housing improvements, access to health care, and prevention. Key limitations include self-reported measures, exclusion of care home residents, and potential influence of unmeasured effects.

records.title: Ambivalent close ties and cognitive functioning: Does coping play a role?
records.abstract: and  Close relationships that are characterized by both positive and negative qualities (i.e., ambivalent ties) are common in later life and often give rise to interpersonal tensions with deleterious consequences for well-being. However, little is known about their effect on cognitive health. These effects may depend on seldom-studied interpersonal coping strategies that may either stimulate or deplete cognitive resources. This study tested whether ambivalent ties relate to lower cognitive functioning among older adults, and whether interpersonal coping strategies moderate these associations. Research Design and  As part of the Daily Experiences and Well-being Study (DEWS), participants (N = 271, ages 65-89) completed an in-person baseline interview assessing positive and negative qualities of their close social relationships and overall cognitive functioning (composite of four tests), followed by a self-administered questionnaire assessing three interpersonal coping strategies (engaged, avoidant, destructive). A greater proportion of ambivalent ties in one’s social network is associated with lower cognitive functioning among older adults, a link that may not easily be buffered through coping.  suggest that ambivalent ties are an understudied important potential risk factor for adverse cognitive outcomes in later life.

records.title: Changes in Instrumental Support Around Retirement: Longitudinal Evidence From Europe
records.abstract: As populations age and the share of retirees increases across Europe, the question of whether individuals stay active after retirement is increasingly salient. These findings indicate that retirement may promote activity and facilitate engagement in helping others.

This study aimed to update the comparative effectiveness of 5 technology categories—exergaming with balance platforms (EBP), exergaming with motion capture (EMC), other serious games, interventions with wearables, and telerehabilitation (Tele)—versus conventional exercise (CE), and no treatment (NT), applying GRADE adapted for NMA. Fifty-seven trials (2758 analyzed participants) contributed to 4 prespecified networks (all balance, functional scales, Timed Up and Go [TUG] test, and gait speed). A random-effects NMA was fitted using multivariate meta-regression. Treatment hierarchies were summarized by the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) and the probability of being best; certainty of evidence was rated with GRADE adapted for NMA. Tele, EBP, and EMC were each associated with improved balance versus NT, although none exceeded CE. The first-place SUCRA ranking of Tele is preliminary. Certainty was moderate only for EBP and EMC versus NT on the TUG test; the remaining evidence is too uncertain for firm clinical recommendations. As no included trial reported falls, these findings are not direct evidence of fall prevention. Larger trials with standardized comparator intensity and posttraining follow-up are required.

records.title: Feasibility of a Co-Designed Personalized Cognitive Reablement Program Delivered via Digital Voice Assistants for Older Adults Living With Early-Stage Dementia or Mild Cognitive Impairment: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial
records.abstract: Home-based reablement programs have improved everyday functioning for people living with early-stage dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but the substantial time commitment required for delivery by health professionals has created a barrier to widespread implementation. Digital technology could facilitate delivery, but traditional devices such as smartphones and tablets present usability challenges for this population. We have co-designed a cognitive reablement program, VOICE-COG, that can deliver personalized interventions broadcast via voice-controlled digital voice assistants (DVAs).  This pilot nonblinded randomized controlled trial examined the feasibility and potential effectiveness of VOICE-COG for older adults living with dementia or MCI to guide the design of a full-scale trial.  Older adults (aged 60‐85 years) with a self-reported diagnosis of dementia or MCI (N=30) were recruited via Facebook or the StepUp-for Dementia Research database and randomized to either a DVA intervention (n=15) or control (n=15) group for 12 weeks. Each participant randomized to the intervention group and their care partner met with a psychologist via Zoom to select 2 or 3 personalized goals from the VOICE-COG program. The personalized program was input into the software (BuddyLink) by researchers for broadcast via a DVA (Amazon Alexa Show 8). Participants in the control group received enhanced usual care, consisting of treatment as usual, plus weekly informational emails. Primary feasibility outcomes were recruitment, retention, device-recorded adherence, and the System Usability Scale (SUS). Secondary outcomes were self-reported by the participant and care partner via web-based Qualtrics forms and included the Goal Attainment Scale–Light (GAS), changes in participant mood, cognition, and everyday functioning, and carer burden.  The recruitment rate was 86% (30/35) and the retention rate was 97% (29/30), with 1 participant in the intervention group lost to follow-up. Adherence to the VOICE-COG program ranged from 29% to 100% (mean 70%, SD 17%). The VOICE-COG program was rated as marginally acceptable (mean SUS score 56.3, SD 18.1). After 12 weeks, 60% (9/15) of the intervention group reported having met or exceeded their goals (GAS-Light t-score ≥50; mean 57.6, SD 15.4). The intervention group had a significantly higher increase in Multifactorial Memory Questionnaire–Strategy subscale score compared with control, mean difference 5.0 (95% CI 0.03-10.1, P =.049), representing a medium effect size ( d =0.55). There were no other significant differences between groups.  This co-designed VOICE-COG program, delivered via DVAs, was feasible for older adults living with early-stage dementia or MCI, resulting in most participants meeting their reablement goals and increases in the use of memory strategies. System usability issues should be addressed in future adequately powered trials.

records.title: Age trajectories of informal caregiving for older people in England: Testing the healthy caregiver hypothesis
records.abstract: and  This study investigates how health status shapes the age trajectories of informal caregiving for spouses and older parents in England. Research Design and  The data came from five waves (2012–2023) of the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA). We analysed 41,997 person-wave observations from 12,420 individuals aged 50+. We derived a latent health construct via hierarchical confirmatory factor analysis, integrating functional, mental, physical, and cognitive domains. Dynamic random-effects models were employed to examine the influence of prior health on consequent caregiving, and initial condition adjustment was made to correct estimation bias.  Among those with a spouse, parents, or parents-in-law, healthier individuals demonstrated steeper increases in caregiving probability over time, while those in poor health showed flatter or declining caregiving trajectories. For spousal caregiving, better health was associated with a lower likelihood of caregiving at age 50, but this relationship turned positive from age 70 onwards. For parental caregiving, better health was associated with a higher likelihood of caregiving from age 53 onwards.  Overall the research findings are consistent with the healthy caregiver hypothesis, particularly in later life. Good health facilitates the provision of informal care, whereas poor health compromises caregiving capability and constitutes a barrier to taking on a caregiving role. A healthier older population not only means lower care needs but also has greater capacity to provide care.

records.title: Emergent Connections: A Community-Based Model for Advancing Social Connection Among Immigrant Older Adults with Disabilities
records.abstract: and  Social isolation is an urgent public health concern, especially for older immigrants who face heightened barriers to social participation due to disability, structural health inequities, and limited access to culturally and linguistically appropriate services. This study presents a programmatic model that explains how social connection and sustained participation can be fostered through accessible, culturally responsive, and participatory design. Research Design and  This community-engaged case study examines a national virtual program serving Spanish-speaking older adults, many of whom have sensory disabilities and chronic illnesses. A thematic and comparative analysis was conducted using qualitative interviews with ten older adults with vision impairment, program documents, and consultation with program leadership. This led to the identification of a programmatic model, the emergent connections platform.  The emergent connections platform strengthens loosely connected social networks among older adults who share cultural and lived experiences through three pillars. The first is cultural, linguistic, and physically accessible infrastructure. Second, shared governance cultivates member leadership and program co-creation. Third, a flexible structure allows for evolution in response to member needs and innovations. These pillars collectively create pathways for individuals to engage, lead, and strengthen their communities.  Advancing a more inclusive democracy requires sustained investment in accessible, community-led initiatives that support the leadership and innovation of marginalized older adults. This calls for moving towards models that position older adults as co-creators of programs and services. Doing so cultivates social connection through leadership, reciprocity, and a sense of belonging within a broader social fabric.

records.title: Determinants of Self-Care Practices Among Family Caregivers of Older Adults with Chronic Illness: A Qualitative Descriptive Study
records.abstract: and  Caregiver burden significantly impedes self-care, often resulting in poor health and increased vulnerability to chronic illness. Despite these risks, the underlying factors influencing caregivers’ self-care remain understudied. This qualitative descriptive study explored the context of caregiver self-care and identified perceived barriers and facilitators to practicing self-care. Research Design and  We conducted four focus groups with 14 caregivers primarily responsible for providing in-home care to older adults (≥ 65 years) with chronic illnesses. Focus groups were audio-recorded and transcribed. A hierarchical coding system was developed and refined using the focus group guide and preliminary transcript review. Coded transcripts were analyzed using an iterative inductive-deductive thematic approach based on established theories.  Caregivers’ multi-dimensional definitions of self-care shaped their perceived barriers and facilitators. Three core determinants of self-care behaviors were identified: capability (caregivers’ psychological and physical health, and behavioral regulation); motivation (caregiver identity, emotions, and perceived control); and opportunity (social and environmental influences and resources). Caregivers recognized that self-care deficits negatively affect their clinical, behavioral, and psychosocial outcomes. These  informed the development of a conceptual framework for caregiver self-care.  Findings underscore the importance of integrating caregivers’ own perceptions of self-care into support models. Interventions should transition toward personalized approaches that address both intrinsic psychological drivers and extrinsic environmental constraints. The framework derived from this study provides a theory-driven roadmap that informs future interventions, ensuring support systems align with caregivers’ unique needs and contexts to foster better self-care and ultimately enhance their health outcomes.

records.title: Drafting the next chapter: A scoping review of academic retirement planning
records.abstract: and  Interest in retirement planning among university faculty has grown in recent years as more academics approach traditional retirement age. This scoping review examines the current literature on retirement planning among higher education faculty by examining study characteristics; participant characteristics; theoretical frameworks employed; factors influencing retirement planning; and the quality of the included studies. Research Design and  A comprehensive search across Medline, Embase, APA PsycInfo, AgeLine, ERIC, Education Source, Business Source Premier, Sociological Abstracts, International Bibliography of the Social Sciences, JSTOR, and Web of Science Core Collection yielded an initial dataset of 8,906 unique articles. Following full-text assessment, 44 studies met the inclusion criteria.  Five factors prevailed across this literature as key mechanisms in academic retirement planning, including: 1) financial security; 2) health factors; 3) age and/or institutional policies; 4) work, family, and lifestyle factors; and 5) professional identity. Participant characteristics such as age, gender, stage of retirement, and other characteristics of the academic environment were reported inconsistently across the literature; only 14 of the studies mentioned a theoretical framework.  This is the first scoping review of academic retirement with a focus on planning that includes a range of . While health and financial security remain central to retirement planning broadly, the studies in this review suggest that professional identity plays a distinct role in shaping how academics approach retirement planning. Implications include the need for longitudinal designs to capture how faculty transitions, shifting professional identities, and planning behaviors evolve dynamically over time.

records.title: Practice Effects on Repeated Self-Administered Digital Cognitive Assessments in Cognitively Intact Older Adults from the Framingham Heart Study: Longitudinal Observational Study
records.abstract: Remote, self-administered digital assessments provide scalable approaches for monitoring cognition in older adults. Practice effects (PEs), once viewed as measurement noise, are increasingly recognized as potential markers of cognitive decline. As disease-modifying therapies for neurodegenerative conditions emerge, longitudinal digital assessments may capture subtle cognitive changes. Although the majority of PE studies have focused on memory tasks, it is critical to determine whether PEs occur in other domains. Clarifying the potential presence of PEs across multiple time points on the Food and Drug Administration–cleared Defense Automated Neurocognitive Assessment (DANA) platform remains critical for determining whether PEs can serve as a measure of cognitive decline longitudinally.  This study aimed to examine whether PEs occur and whether demographics moderate them across quarterly self-administrations of digital cognitive tasks spanning different cognitive domains in cognitively intact older adults.  Cognitively intact older adults from the Framingham Heart Study self-administered DANA tasks at baseline and every 3 months for 1 year (4 assessments: T1-T4). Tasks included Simple Reaction Time (SRT), Go/No-Go (GNG), and Code Substitution (CS). These tasks varied in complexity, from simple motor responding (SRT) to inhibitory control (GNG) and associative learning with working memory demands (CS).
